The first thing that comes is a window.

Not a grand window. No cathedral glass, no ships beyond it. Just a fourth-floor window with a paint-chipped latch, overlooking a courtyard where someone has planted tomatoes in an old bathtub. It is 4:17 in the afternoon, that neglected hour when the day has spent its ambitions but has not yet admitted it is tired.

Across the courtyard, an old man comes out wearing yellow socks and feeds the pigeons. He has named them after composers. Beethoven is fat and belligerent. Clara Schumann waits apart on the sill. Mozart arrives late, takes what he wants, and leaves without apology. The old man scolds them in a language I do not know, and they repent without changing their behavior.

On my table is a list of things I meant to do: mend the blue shirt; learn twelve Portuguese verbs; call Mara; be less afraid. The last item is too large for the paper. I have crossed it out and written it back so many times that it has become a small black weather system.

I have kept the window shut for weeks, though the room has done nothing to deserve this. Dust has gathered on the latch. A plant beside the glass has leaned so insistently toward the light that its whole body seems to be asking a question.

We are taught to watch for turning points, as if they should arrive with music, or at least with weather. We expect the doorbell, the diagnosis, the letter slipped beneath the door. But most changes begin in clothes too ordinary to remember afterward. Someone puts on a kettle. Someone picks up the keys. Someone decides that today, for no defensible reason, they will not continue in quite the same direction.

When we were children, my sister Mara and I shared a red umbrella. She always held it slightly over me, which meant that by the time we reached school, one of her sleeves was soaked. I remembered this only recently, after spending several years remembering the ways she had disappointed me. Memory is a careless accountant. It enters some debts twice and misplaces entire fortunes of kindness.

Now rain begins, so lightly that at first it seems to be a thought the courtyard is having. The old man looks up. The pigeons do not. Rain darkens his shoulders and silvers the tomatoes. He laughs once, gathers his paper bag, and goes inside.

I stand and open the window.

The smell that rises is not exactly rain. It is dust remembering it was once earth. Somewhere below, a radio changes stations. A saucepan falls. A child says, “Again,” with the absolute conviction that joy can be commanded.

A sentence, I think, is a window with better manners. It says: here is the wall, and here is the place I have cut through it. Look. It cannot make you climb through. It cannot promise weather you will like. It can only insist that the room is not the whole world.

I call Mara.

She answers on the fourth ring.

“Hello?”

“It’s me.”

There is a pause, but it is not empty. It is a small room with both of us standing in it.

“I know,” she says. “Your name came up.”

This makes me laugh, though I am close to crying, and the nearness of those two things surprises me.

“How have you been?”

“The tap is still leaking.”

“Still?”

“It has become philosophical. It drips only when I stop listening.”

I tell her about Beethoven and the tomatoes. She tells me our cousin has bought a goat for reasons no one has been able to establish. We do not mention the year and a half, or the last message, which was too careful to be kind. We do not perform the difficult surgery of the past. We simply keep the line open between us while she washes something in the sink and I watch rain collect along the railing.

Before we hang up, she says, “It’s good you called.” Not like forgiveness, exactly. More like a hand left on a doorframe.

Afterward, nothing looks transformed. The old man does not return. The plant has not produced a miraculous leaf. My list is still there, creased and faintly accusing. But one item now has a clean line through it, and the line does not resemble weather. It resembles a road.

Outside, a pigeon crosses the courtyard and lands on my sill. It is probably Clara Schumann, though I cannot be sure. We regard each other with the mutual suspicion of creatures who have both expected bread.

Perhaps courage is usually this unimpressive: a window lifted, a number dialed, two people discussing a tap while something enormous quietly changes its mind.

The first thing that comes is a window. The second is rain. The third, if I am lucky, is the small, ordinary willingness to open.
